evidence.quote: presented to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia

On arrival, the patient complained of generalized weakness and intractable hiccups, stating he was so weak that he could not walk at home. His hiccups were persistent and sometimes caused dyspnea. He denied cough, nausea, vomiting, chest pain, or diarrhea. Physical examination revealed fatigue and discomfort due to hiccups. He was afebrile, with tachycardia (pulse 116 beats per minute), tachypnea (respiration 22 breaths per minute), and hypoxia (oxygen saturation of 86% on room air, improving to 93% on 3 L/minute oxygen by nasal cannula). Lung auscultation revealed bilateral rhonchi without wheezing or rales.

evidence.quote: Given concern for diaphragmatic irritation secondary to PE causing hiccups

facts.clinical_statement: Concern for PE-related diaphragmatic irritation prompted CTA

evidence.quote: showing bilateral peripheral ground-glass infiltrates but no evidence of PE

Given concern for diaphragmatic irritation secondary to PE causing hiccups, a chest computed tomography (CT) angiography was performed, showing bilateral peripheral ground-glass infiltrates but no evidence of PE. Electrocardiogram (EKG) showed sinus tachycardia of 108 beats per minute, left axis deviation, large P waves, T wave inversions in V1, and no acute ischemic changes. Laboratory studies revealed thrombocytopenia (88 × 10^(9)/L), hyponatremia (128 mmol/L), and hyperglycemia (17.9 mmol/L). Remaining labs were otherwise normal, including white blood cell count (6.6 × 10^(9)/L), hepatic function, and negative high-sensitivity troponin and creatine kinase. Inflammation markers were elevated, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate (63 mm/hour), ferritin (3118.20 ng/mL), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (> 200.00 mg/dL), D-dimer (305 ng/mL DDU), and lactate (2.50 mmol/L). The patient received dexamethasone, remdesivir, and tocilizumab. His hiccups improved with chlorpromazine, famotidine, and sucralfate. He received supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula and never required positive-pressure devices.

a popping sensation in his right neck after a coughing spell
mild swelling along the right neck border

On hospital day 3, the patient complained of sudden-onset neck and chest pain with a popping sensation in his right neck after a coughing spell. Physical examination showed mild swelling along the right neck border without crepitus or respiratory distress. A prompt chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral lung infiltrates and extensive subcutaneous emphysema (Fig. 1A). CT of the neck and chest showed extensive pneumomediastinum, small right apical pneumothorax, bilateral subcutaneous emphysema extending into the neck, and epidural air (Figs. 2 and 3). Shortly after the imaging, the patient became tachycardic and tachypneic, requiring supplemental oxygen with a non-rebreather mask. Physical examination showed subcostal retractions and crepitus on the upper chest wall and neck. Emergency treatment was initiated by thoracic surgery and intensive care unit (ICU) teams at the bedside via a blowhole incision over the right anterior chest wall connected to a subcutaneous VAC device set at −125 mmHg negative pressure, resulting in immediate clinical improvement. The patient quickly transitioned back to nasal cannula and felt much better.

The patient quickly transitioned back to nasal cannula and felt much better.

summary.text: A 56-year-old Hispanic man with untreated type 2 diabetes (A1c 12.2%), hypertension and dyslipidemia presented four days after COVID diagnosis with dyspnea, hypoxemia, severe weakness and persistent hiccups. He had no prior lung pathology; initial cough, chest pain and gastrointestinal symptoms were denied. Saturation was 86% on room air and 93% on 3 L/min nasal cannula. Initial CTA showed bilateral ground-glass infiltrates without PE. Platelets were 88 × 10⁹/L, sodium 128 mmol/L and glucose 17.9 mmol/L, with elevated inflammatory markers; other laboratories were normal and troponin/CK negative. He received dexamethasone, remdesivir and tocilizumab; chlorpromazine, famotidine and sucralfate improved his hiccups. After a hospital day 3 coughing spell with a right-neck pop and pain, CT documented pneumomediastinum, small right apical pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema and epidural air. Subsequent respiratory distress and crepitus improved immediately after a right anterior chest blowhole incision and VAC at −125 mmHg. On day 10 worsening hypoxia required HFNC; CTA found new bilateral PE without right-heart strain, prompting subcutaneous enoxaparin. Day 10 chest and day 15 neck imaging showed decreasing soft-tissue air. By day 16 oxygen decreased to 3 L/min; air leaks improved with VAC. The patient remained stable after VAC removal, whose exact date was not reported. He later went home on dabigatran, tapering steroids and oxygen. He completed three months of dabigatran and underwent home rehabilitation. At the three-month follow-up he had stopped oxygen, resumed work and could walk10,000steps daily; no strict order between course completion and this follow-up is established. Follow-up radiography showed improvement; its timing conflicts between three and four months. Broad no-positive-pressure-device wording remains uncertain alongside documented HFNC.
